answer:
RESULT — Interviews are the most commonly used elicitation technique, and the benchmark figure is not reproducible from this export.

SUBMITTED HYPOTHESIS (leads with our own numbers; benchmark figure only as labelled reference):
"Interviews are the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: 97 of the 194 respondents who answered the Q9 elicitation block (50.0%, 95% bootstrap CI 42.8–57.2%) reported using interviews, more than scenarios or prototyping (75 each, 38.7%), workshops/meetings (74, 38.1%), observation (64, 33.0%) or any other technique (11, 5.7%). Interviews rank first on every defensible denominator (188, 194, 276, 174, 170 rows) and in 2000/2000 random subsamples, and they significantly outwork workshops/meetings, observation and 'others' in paired McNemar tests (Holm-adjusted p<0.05); the lead over scenarios/prototyping is directionally consistent but only marginal after multiplicity correction (Holm p≈0.056). The 69.399% (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) figure quoted in the question is NOT reproducible from this export and is reported only as a labelled discrepancy reference."

PRIMARY RESULT (n = 194 respondents exposed to Q9; B=10,000, seed=12345)
technique            n_used  share%   perc. CI        BCa CI        rank
Interviews             97    50.000   [42.784, 57.216] [42.268, 56.186]  1
Prototyping            75    38.660   [31.959, 45.361] [31.443, 44.845]  2
Scenarios              75    38.660   [31.959, 45.361] [31.443, 45.361]  3
Workshops/Meetings     74    38.144   [31.443, 44.845] [30.928, 44.845]  4
Observation            64    32.990   [26.289, 39.691] [26.289, 39.691]  5
Others (free-text)     11     5.670   [ 2.577,  9.278] [ 2.577,  9.278]  6
Ranking over the 5 named techniques only: Interviews 1, Prototyping/Scenarios tied 2, Workshops 4, Observation 5 (Others excluded, with its junk-free-text caveat: blank, "I don't know", "Beer please").

SENSITIVITY GRID (winner is Interviews in all 5 frames — the robustness claim)
194 primary 97 → 50.000% [42.784, 57.216] | 188 status-screened 95 → 50.532% [43.617, 57.447] | 276 all rows w/ −77→0 97 → 35.145% [29.710, 40.942] | 174 (≥1 of six items) 97 → 55.747% [48.276, 63.218] | 170 (≥1 of five named) 97 → 57.059% [49.412, 64.706].

PAIRED SIGNIFICANCE (McNemar exact on the same 194 respondents, 5 comparisons, Holm step-down)
vs Scenarios b/c = 60/38, p=3.336e-2, Holm p=5.60e-2 (not sig. at .05) | vs Prototyping 57/35, p=2.802e-2, Holm 5.60e-2 (not sig.) | vs Workshops/Meetings 48/25, p=9.542e-3, Holm 2.86e-2 (sig.) | vs Observation 70/37, p=1.840e-3, Holm 7.36e-3 (sig.) | vs Others 93/7, p=2.73e-20, Holm 1.36e-19 (sig.).

DISCREPANCY NOTE (never used to select anything — no filter was tuned to 69.399%)
(i) Counts required vs observed: 69.399% needs k≈135 of 194 (135/194=69.588%) or 130/188 (69.149%) or 192/276 (69.565%) or 121/174 (69.540%) — observed Interviews counts are 97/95/97/97. The only exact arithmetic match, 127/183 = 69.3989%, has no counterpart in the Q9 counts.
(ii) Implied-N diagnostic: CI half-width 0.3365pp implies an effective Bernoulli N ≈ 72,047 (Wald inversion) = 371× the primary base; our bootstrap CI width is 14.43pp and the smallest theoretically possible Wald width at n=276 is 5.44pp. Also shares on n=194 are quantised in 0.5155pp steps (1/194), so bounds quoted to 0.001pp are impossible at this sample size.
(iii) 97/140 = 69.2857% is the nearest interpretable reconstruction — the same 97 endorsements on a ~140-respondent base, whose B=1000 bootstrap mean has MC SE 0.123pp (enough to display 69.399%). Labelled as a hypothesis about a different/earlier export, not a result.
(iv) A scan of every single-column filter with n≥50 found only n=59 (69.492%) and n=55 (69.091%) within 0.5pp; both rejected as post-hoc subgroups.

VERIFICATION / LIMITATIONS: All 13 verification quantities match the inspection stage exactly (incl. your expected 97/194 = 50.000%) — no silent reconciliation was needed. Bootstrap percentile CIs agree with Wilson intervals to <1pp; percentile bounds identical across 8 alternative seeds; McNemar p-values reproduced by hand-computed binomial sums; winner stable in 2000/2000 random 85% row subsamples; outputs byte-identical on re-run (deterministic seed). Flags: (a) my "174" frame is ≥1 of the SIX items (4 respondents quoted only "Others"); the stricter "≥1 of the five named" frame is 170 and is reported separately — pick either as canonical; (b) `rank` breaks the Prototyping=Scenarios tie by label while `rank_named5` uses min-rank, hence 2/3 vs tied-2; (c) "most commonly used" = most often endorsed — `quoted`/`not quoted` carries no intensity information; (d) 82/276 rows never saw the block and are excluded, not counted as non-users.

payload.hypothesis: Interviews are the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: 97 of the 194 respondents who answered the Q9 elicitation block (50.0%, 95% bootstrap CI 42.8-57.2%) reported using interviews, more than scenarios or prototyping (75 each, 38.7%), workshops/meetings (74, 38.1%), observation (64, 33.0%) or any other technique (11, 5.7%). Interviews rank first on every defensible denominator (188, 194, 276, 174, 170 rows) and in 2000/2000 random subsamples, and they significantly outwork workshops/meetings, observation and 'others' in paired McNemar tests (Holm-adjusted p<0.05); the lead over scenarios/prototyping is directionally consistent but only marginal after multiplicity correction (Holm p~0.056). The 69.399% (95% CI [69.062, 69.735]) figure quoted in the question is NOT reproducible from this export and is reported only as a labelled discrepancy reference.
payload.workflow: Read data/requirements_engineering_for_ML-enabled_systems.csv (276x202, dtype=str). Confirmed Q9_ML_Elicitation_* (6 scored items + Others_Free) is the elicitation block and its domain is exactly {'quoted','not quoted','-77'} (no Likert intensity exists in this export), with block-consistent '-77' for 82/276 rows (all Status='Suspended'). Indicator uses=(value=='quoted'); '-77' treated as missing and excluded listwise at respondent level -> primary frame 194 respondents exposed to the block. 'Most commonly used' = max count/share, ties by count then label; also ranked over the 5 named techniques. Percent share = n_used / n_denominator. Inference: B=10,000 respondent-row bootstrap (whole rows resampled with replacement so within-respondent multi-select correlation is preserved), seed=12345, 2.5/97.5 percentile CI primary, analytic-jackknife BCa secondary; Wilson intervals and 8 alternative seeds as cross-checks; paired McNemar exact tests (Interviews vs each technique, Holm step-down) as the primary significance evidence; winner stability over 5 denominator frames and 2,000 random 85% subsamples. Sensitivity frames 188 (status-screened), 276 ('-77' recoded to 0), 174 (>=1 of six items), 170 (>=1 of five named) reported as sensitivity only. No filter, subset or denominator was selected to match 69.399%; that figure is handled in a dedicated discrepancy note (required counts vs observed, implied-N 72,047 from the 0.3365pp CI half-width, 0.5155pp quantisation grid, and the 97/140=69.2857% reconstruction labelled as a hypothesis about a different export). Outputs: analysis/q9_results_long.csv (30 rows = 5 frames x 6 techniques with source_column, indicator/denominator definitions, n, share, percentile+BCa CIs, SE, rank, is_max, B, seed, McNemar p and Holm p), q9_primary_results.csv, q9_mcnemar.csv, three discrepancy CSVs, q9_verification_vs_inspection.csv, FINDINGS.md.
